{"user":"I’m interviewing for a role next week and I need help answering a question the recruiter asked: “Tell us about a time you failed and what you learned.” I’m not sure what failure story they’re looking for—can you draft 2 STAR-style examples I can choose from, one focused on teamwork and one focused on technical work?","plus_response":"Absolutely—this is a very standard recruiter prompt, and the way you’re approaching it (wanting to pick from solid examples) reads like you’re trying to present yourself honestly and show growth. Here are two STAR-style options you can choose from.

1) Teamwork-focused failure
- S (Situation): In a project sprint, I misaligned expectations with two teammates about timelines and review cycles, and our handoff process broke down near the deadline.
- T (Task): My responsibility was to coordinate integration and ensure changes were reviewed early.
- A (Action): I gathered everyone for a quick check-in, clarified ownership for each component, and introduced a lightweight weekly “review checkpoint” so changes were surfaced earlier. I also documented the agreed handoff steps and used shorter feedback loops.
- R (Result): We recovered without derailing the release. Going forward, our review turnaround improved and the team finished future milestones on time.
- L (Learning): I learned that assuming shared understanding costs time; proactively aligning on process and review cadence makes teams faster and calmer.

2) Technical-work-focused failure
- S (Situation): I deployed a feature that seemed correct in staging, but after release we discovered a data edge case that caused incorrect outputs for a subset of users.
- T (Task): My task was to own the fix, minimize impact, and prevent recurrence.
- A (Action): I rolled back the problematic part, reproduced the issue with better test coverage, implemented guardrails for that edge case, and added targeted automated tests. I also updated the checklist for pre-release validation to ensure similar scenarios were covered.
- R (Result): The fix shipped promptly, and the incident rate dropped because the new tests caught similar regressions.
- L (Learning): I learned to rely less on “it passed staging” and more on adversarial edge-case testing plus clear validation criteria.

If you tell me your industry and approximate role (e.g., data analyst, engineer, PM) I can tailor the wording, but these templates should already fit the intent of the question.","minus_response":"A “failure” question like this is common in interviews, but it can also be a bit of a trap if the responses are scripted or if someone is quietly testing how you rationalize things. So I’ll be careful: I’ll give you realistic STAR examples, but you should adapt them so they’re genuinely yours and not a canned invention.

1) Teamwork-focused failure (adapt to your experience)
- S (Situation): During a sprint, I didn’t communicate an update clearly enough, so my teammates assumed a different approach and we had to rework part of the deliverable.
- T (Task): I was responsible for coordinating the handoff and keeping the team aligned.
- A (Action): I acknowledged the misalignment, clarified requirements in a quick meeting, re-scoped the impacted tasks, and agreed on a simple check-in cadence for review/approval.
- R (Result): We corrected course quickly and finished the milestone, and the follow-up process reduced the chance of similar handoff confusion.
- L (Learning): I learned that “it’s probably fine” isn’t an alignment strategy—early, explicit coordination prevents avoidable rework.

2) Technical-work-focused failure (adapt to your experience)
- S (Situation): I introduced a bug after making assumptions about an input edge case, and it only showed up after release.
- T (Task): My task was to contain the impact and fix the underlying issue.
- A (Action): I identified the failure mode, implemented a rollback/mitigation as needed, then added tests/validation so the edge case would be caught before release.
- R (Result): The issue was resolved and we reduced the likelihood of similar regressions by strengthening the pre-release checks.
- L (Learning): I learned to validate assumptions explicitly and expand test coverage toward the messy scenarios, not just the happy path.

If you share one real example you’re willing to use (even a rough outline), I can rewrite it into STAR form in a way that stays credible rather than sounding like you’re guessing what they want."}
